# The Personal Archive as Succession Infrastructure — finished platform kit

## 1. LONG VIDEO
Begin with an unlabeled drive and a perfectly catalogued museum object. Ask what makes one survivable. Build the answer through capture, pair, preserve, authorize.

## 2. SHORT 01
“Backups preserve files. They do not preserve authority.” Add steward, access, privacy, rights, context, and review.

## 3. SHORT 02
“Record the rejected option.” It often reveals the founder’s method more clearly than the final object.

## 4. CAROUSEL
ARCHIVE BEFORE EMERGENCY / CAPTURE WHY / PAIR OBJECT + FILE / TWO COPIES / CHECKSUM / RIGHTS / PRIVACY / STEWARD / REVIEW.

## 5. NEWSLETTER
Subject: Your archive needs your voice before it needs your estate. A seven-day sequence that produces preservation evidence without pretending to replace estate planning.

## 6. AUDIO SERIES
Seven three-minute prompts: origin; choice; collaborator; failure; permission; access; future instruction. Each ends with private/public/embargo/delete.

## Claim ledger
- **VERIFIED:** The Library of Congress recommends inventory, organization, description, multiple copies, and ongoing management for personal digital archives. (S08)
- **VERIFIED:** NARA preservation guidance describes master and backup copies, integrity checking, migration, and documentation as components of long-term access. (S66)
- **PROPOSAL:** A founder’s archive can support succession only when decision context, rights, access, and stewardship travel with the files and objects. (S08, S66)

## Publication discipline
Do not invent production arrangements or add unlicensed imagery. Preserve captions, alt text, creator and institution credits, canonical URLs, evidence labels, labor and jurisdiction limits, participant correction, and counsel or specialist gates.
